title: Reduced graph closure extending a projective generic map
statement:
Let $k$ be a field and $S$ an integral separated scheme of finite type over $k$, with generic point $\eta$ and function field $K$. Let $L/K$ be finite separable. Suppose $q:N\to S$ is finite and surjective with $N$ normal integral of finite type over $k$, equipped with a generic-point map $j:\operatorname{Spec}L\to N$ identifying $k(N)$ with $L$ as a $K$-extension, such that $j$ induces an isomorphism $\operatorname{Spec}L\simeq N\times_S\operatorname{Spec}K$. Let $M$ be a projective finite-type $k$-scheme and $a:\operatorname{Spec}L\to M$ a $k$-morphism. Set $Q=M\times_k N$, let $x$ be the image of $(a,j):\operatorname{Spec}L\to Q$, and let $i:T\hookrightarrow Q$ be the reduced induced closed subscheme on $\overline{\{x\}}$. Then $T$ is integral, and $(a,j)$ factors as $i\circ j_T$ with $j_T:\operatorname{Spec}L\to T$ its generic-point map. The projection $b:T\to N$ is proper and surjective, and the induced map $\operatorname{Spec}L\to T\times_N\operatorname{Spec}L$ is an isomorphism over $L$. The composite $r=q\circ b:T\to S$ is proper, surjective and of finite type; for some dense open $V\subseteq S$, $r^{-1}(V)\to V$ is finite. Its induced function-field extension is identified with $L/K$ via $j_T$, and $m=\operatorname{pr}_M\circ i:T\to M$ satisfies $m\circ j_T=a$.

Here normal means that all local rings are integrally closed domains; separated means that the diagonal is a closed immersion. Reduced induced closed subschemes use [lem-weil-pbc-reduced-induced-closed-subscheme]; closed immersions and projectivity use [def-weil-closed-immersion] and [def-kun-projective]. The remaining notions use [def-weil-field], [def-pc-scheme], [def-pc-integral-scheme], [def-weil-finite-type-morphism], [def-weil-finite-integral-morphism], [def-weil-surjective-morphism], [def-weil-proper-morphism], [def-sc-function-field], [def-pc-field-extension], [def-weil-pbc-separable-algebraic-extension], [def-pc-fibre-product] and [def-sc-generic-point].

proof.text: Write $h=(a,j)$. The closure of the single point $x$ is nonempty and irreducible: two open subsets meeting it both contain $x$ and therefore meet. The reduced-induced-subscheme lemma makes $T$ reduced, so the integral-scheme criterion makes $T$ integral, with generic point $x_T=i^{-1}(x)$. On an affine open $U=\operatorname{Spec}R$ of $Q$ containing $x$, write $\varphi:R\to L$ for $h$. The point $x$ corresponds to the prime $\mathfrak p=\ker\varphi$ and $\overline{\{x\}}\cap U=V(\mathfrak p)$. The reduced-induced-subscheme lemma gives $i^{-1}U=\operatorname{Spec}(R/\mathfrak p)$. Thus $\varphi$ factors through $R/\mathfrak p\hookrightarrow L$, and these local factorizations glue uniquely (on affine overlaps they are the same quotient factorization). This defines $j_T$ with $ij_T=h$ and image $x_T$.

source.place: Tag 01J3, lemma-reduced-closed-subscheme, affine construction; properties.tex Tag 01ON, lemma-characterize-integral

proof.text: Choose an affine open $W=\operatorname{Spec}A$ of $N$ containing its generic point and an affine open $U=\operatorname{Spec}R\subseteq\operatorname{pr}_N^{-1}W$ containing $x$. Put $B=R/\ker(R\to L)$ as in step 1. The composite $A\to B\hookrightarrow L$ is the generic-point inclusion supplied by $j$. The affine fraction-field lemma applied to $N$ gives $\operatorname{Frac}(A)=L$. Consequently $A\subseteq B\subseteq L$ implies $\operatorname{Frac}(B)=L$: a fraction in $B$ lies in $L$, and every element of $L$ is already a fraction of elements of $A$. Apply the same lemma to the integral scheme $T$ and its nonempty affine open $\operatorname{Spec}B$. It identifies $k(T)=\operatorname{Frac}(B)=L$ through the map $j_T$, so $j_T$ is precisely the generic-point map. The induced extension from $k(S)=K$ is the prescribed $L/K$, since $rj_T=qj$ and $j$ respects that $K$-structure.

source.place: Tag 01RV, lemma-integral-scheme-rational-functions; Tag 01RW, definition-function-field; schemes.tex Tag 01HV, lemma-spec-sheaves (6), applied at the prime (0) of a domain

proof.text: Retain $W=\operatorname{Spec}A$ and cover $b^{-1}W$ by its nonempty affine opens $\operatorname{Spec}B_\alpha$. Each contains the generic point of $T$; by step 2 its generic evaluation is injective, so $A\subseteq B_\alpha\subseteq L=\operatorname{Frac}(A)$. The affine fibre-product formula identifies its pullback to $\operatorname{Spec}L$ with $\operatorname{Spec}(B_\alpha\otimes_A L)$. Multiplication $B_\alpha\otimes_A L\to L$, $c\otimes\lambda\mapsto c\lambda$, is an isomorphism with inverse $\lambda\mapsto1\otimes\lambda$: write $c=a/s$ with $a,s\in A$, $s\ne0$, and use $sc=a$ to get $c\otimes\lambda=1\otimes(a\lambda/s)$. These affine pullbacks cover $T\times_N\operatorname{Spec}L$. On each chart the morphism induced by $j_T$ is the displayed multiplication isomorphism, and its inverse is the structural projection. Thus the projection and $j_T$ are inverse globally. This proves the asserted isomorphism over $L$, including the scheme structure of the fibre.

source.place: Tags 01I4 and 01JQ, lemma-fibre-product-affine-schemes and lemma-fibre-product-affines; explicit tensor calculation from step 2

proof.text: Define $m=\operatorname{pr}_M i$. Then $mj_T=\operatorname{pr}_M h=a$ by the defining projection equation for the fibre product. Similarly $bj_T=j$.

The projective morphism $M\to\operatorname{Spec}k$ is proper by projective-implies-proper. Its base change $\operatorname{pr}_N:Q\to N$ is proper by proper base change. Since $i$ is a closed immersion, the closed-immersion-proper lemma applied to this projection makes $b=\operatorname{pr}_N i$ proper. Hence its image is closed, by the definition of universally closed. The equation $bj_T=j$ puts the generic point of $N$ in that image. A closed subset containing the generic point of an integral scheme is the whole scheme, so $b$ is surjective.

source.place: Tags 01WC, 01W4 and 01W5: lemma-locally-projective-proper, lemma-base-change-proper and lemma-closed-immersion-proper

proof.text: The finite morphism $q$ is proper by finite-implies-proper, so $r=qb$ is proper by proper composition. Both factors are surjective, hence so is $r$. Properness includes finite type, giving the finite-type assertion. It also gives quasi-compactness and separatedness. In particular $r$ is quasi-separated: its diagonal is a closed immersion, whose inverse image of an affine open is the spectrum of a quotient ring and hence quasi-compact.

source.place: Tag 01WN, lemma-finite-proper; Tag 01W3, lemma-composition-proper; affine closed-immersion and proper definitions

proof.text: Fibre-product associativity gives $T\times_S\operatorname{Spec}K\simeq T\times_N(N\times_S\operatorname{Spec}K)$. The specified identification $N\times_S\operatorname{Spec}K\simeq\operatorname{Spec}L$ and step 3 therefore identify this fibre with $\operatorname{Spec}L$, compatibly with $j_T$ and the structural map to $\operatorname{Spec}K$. The underlying fibre over $\eta$ is a singleton by the topological-fibre assertion. The spectrum of a field is Noetherian (its only ideals are $0$ and the whole field, and its spectrum is a point); since $S$ is finite type over $k$, finite-type-over-Noetherian makes $S$ Noetherian. Apply the generic-finite-neighbourhood lemma to $r$: it is quasi-compact, quasi-separated and locally of finite type by step 6, $S$ is Noetherian, and its only component has generic point $\eta$ with a finite fibre. It gives a dense open $V\subseteq S$ such that $r^{-1}(V)\to V$ is finite.
